Need for Orchestration: Limits of manual container management at scale

slides.title: Problem At Scale
slides.lead: Starting, stopping and checking a handful of containers by hand is manageable, but a production system runs hundreds of containers across many machines, and manual commands cannot keep up
slides.notes: "Open by asking what happens when the single nginx container from the Docker session becomes three hundred containers across twenty machines. Point out that every manual command now needs to run correctly, every time, on the right host. This gap is the exam hook: orchestration exists because manual operations do not scale."

slides.title: Problem At Scale
slides.lead: Container orchestration is the automated system that decides where containers run, keeps the desired number running, and reconnects them as they move, without a human issuing each command

points.text: Decides container placement across available host machines
Restarts or replaces containers that stop responding

slides.notes: "Open by asking what happens when the single nginx container from the Docker session becomes three hundred containers across twenty machines. Point out that every manual command now needs to run correctly, every time, on the right host. This gap is the exam hook: orchestration exists because manual operations do not scale."

slides.title: Problem At Scale

points.text: Adjusts running container count as demand changes
Keeps networking correct as containers move between hosts

Point out that every manual command now needs to run correctly, every time, on the right host. This gap is the exam hook: orchestration exists because manual operations do not scale."

slides.title: Five Failure Points
slides.lead: Each operation that is trivial for one container becomes error-prone once the fleet and the number of hosts grow, because a human cannot track every container's state in real time

points.text: Placement: choosing the least-loaded host by hand is guesswork
Health: a crashed container needs manual detection and restart
Scaling: adding containers for a traffic spike needs human action

slides.notes: "Walk through one failure point concretely: a container crashes at 2 a.m. and nobody restarts it until someone notices the outage. A frequent interview ask is what problem Kubernetes solves, naming Amazon EKS as where this is solved on AWS."

slides.title: Five Failure Points

points.text: Updates: rolling a new image across many hosts risks downtime
Discovery: a moved container's new address breaks static links

note.text: Kubernetes (K8s) is the orchestration platform the industry has standardised on to solve these limits, run in AWS as the managed Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)

slides.notes: "Walk through one failure point concretely: a container crashes at 2 a.m. and nobody restarts it until someone notices the outage. A frequent interview ask is what problem Kubernetes solves, naming Amazon EKS as where this is solved on AWS."
Kubernetes Architecture: Control plane: API server, scheduler, controller manager & etcd; nodes: kubelet, runtime & kube-proxy

slides.title: Control Plane And Nodes
slides.lead: Kubernetes (K8s), an open-source container-orchestration platform, decides placement and keeps containers running by splitting work between a control plane that decides and worker nodes that execute

points.text: API server: front door for every cluster command
Scheduler: picks a node for each new pod (a pod wraps one or more containers)

slides.notes: "Introduce Kubernetes as the orchestration answer to the manual-scaling problem just discussed. Point to the diagram's two boxes as the whole architecture map before any single piece is opened up."

slides.title: Control Plane And Nodes

points.text: Controller manager: keeps actual state matching desired state
etcd: stores the entire cluster state as key-value data
Kubelet, container runtime and kube-proxy: run pods and route traffic on every node

slides.notes: "Introduce Kubernetes as the orchestration answer to the manual-scaling problem just discussed. Point to the diagram's two boxes as the whole architecture map before any single piece is opened up."

slides.label: Analogy: school principal and teachers
slides.title: Control Plane And Nodes
slides.notes: TR analogy: A school principal decides which teacher takes which class, while teachers go into classrooms and actually teach. In the same way, the control plane decides where work runs, and nodes do the actual work. "Introduce Kubernetes as the orchestration answer to the manual-scaling problem just discussed. Point to the diagram's two boxes as the whole architecture map before any single piece is opened up."

slides.title: Cluster Gateway
slides.lead: Every command sent to the cluster, whether typed by an operator or issued by another control-plane process, first lands on the API server: the only direct entry point into the system

points.text: Exposes RESTful endpoints secured over HTTPS, default port 6443
Authenticates and authorizes each incoming request before acting
Validates object specifications and persists them into etcd
Every other control-plane component talks only through it

slides.notes: "Stress that the API server is the single source of truth operators interact with, equivalent to the managed endpoint Amazon EKS exposes. Interview hook: ask why no component bypasses it directly."

slides.title: Placing And Reconciling
slides.lead: Once the API server accepts a new pod, two more control-plane processes decide where it runs and keep it running the way it was declared

points.text: Scheduler: matches each unscheduled pod to a fitting node
Scoring weighs resource requests, affinity and taint rules

slides.notes: "Explain the scheduler as a one-time placement decision and the controller manager as a continuous watch loop. A common interview question asks what happens if a node suddenly dies: the node controller detects the failure, and the pods are evicted and recreated on healthy nodes."

slides.title: Placing And Reconciling

points.text: Controller manager: runs loops comparing actual state to desired state
Node controller detects a failed node and evicts its pods
Deployment-managed pods are recreated on other nodes

slides.notes: "Explain the scheduler as a one-time placement decision and the controller manager as a continuous watch loop. A common interview question asks what happens if a node suddenly dies: the node controller detects the failure, and the pods are evicted and recreated on healthy nodes."

slides.title: Cluster State Database
slides.lead: Every object the scheduler and controller manager read or write is itself held in etcd, a distributed key-value store that acts as the cluster's single source of truth

points.text: Stores all objects: pods, services, configs and secrets
Replicates across control-plane members using the Raft consensus protocol
Default client port 2379, peer communication on port 2380
Losing etcd data means losing the entire cluster state

slides.notes: "Clarify that only the API server reads and writes etcd directly, never the scheduler or controllers themselves. Exam hook: etcd backup and restore is the standard disaster-recovery question for a cluster."

slides.title: Kubelet Runtime Proxy
slides.lead: While the control plane decides, each worker node runs three processes that actually execute containers and route their traffic

points.text: Kubelet: node agent that runs the pods it is assigned
Container runtime: pulls images and starts containers, such as containerd
Kube-proxy: maintains network rules for service traffic routing
Kubelet reports node and pod health back to the API server

slides.notes: "Note that the container runtime is the same containerd layer already met underneath Docker, now managed by kubelet instead of the Docker daemon. Point out kube-proxy as the piece that makes a service address stable despite pods moving."
Pods: The smallest deployable unit; multi-container pods; pod lifecycle & restart policy

slides.title: Smallest Deploy Unit
slides.lead: A container image alone cannot be scheduled on a cluster; Kubernetes needs a wrapper that carries networking and storage context. That wrapper is the Pod: the smallest deployable unit Kubernetes schedules

points.text: Pod wraps one or more containers as a single unit
All containers in a pod share one IP address

slides.notes: "Stress that Kubernetes never schedules a bare container, only a pod. Point out the shared IP as the reason containers inside talk over localhost. Exam hook: why can two containers in one pod not use the same port."

slides.title: Smallest Deploy Unit

points.text: Containers in a pod can share mounted storage volumes
Kubernetes schedules and removes whole pods, never a bare container

slides.notes: "Stress that Kubernetes never schedules a bare container, only a pod. Point out the shared IP as the reason containers inside talk over localhost. Exam hook: why can two containers in one pod not use the same port."

slides.label: Analogy: PG room shared by flatmates
slides.title: Smallest Deploy Unit
slides.notes: TR analogy: A pod is like one PG room shared by flatmates: they share the same address and same kitchen, exactly as pod containers share one IP and one set of volumes. "Stress that Kubernetes never schedules a bare container, only a pod. Point out the shared IP as the reason containers inside talk over localhost. Exam hook: why can two containers in one pod not use the same port."

slides.title: Sidecar And Init
slides.lead: Most pods run a single container, but a pod can bundle helper containers that support the main one without changing its image

points.text: Sidecar: helper container running alongside, e.g. log shipper
Init container: runs once, finishes before app container starts
Ambassador: proxies the main container's outbound network calls

slides.notes: "Explain a sidecar with a concrete example: a logging agent reading the app's log file from a shared volume. Mention Amazon EKS as the AWS service that runs these pod specs. Exam hook: difference between init container and sidecar container."

slides.title: Phases And Transitions
slides.lead: Once created, a pod moves through a fixed sequence of phases that report whether its containers are scheduled, starting or finished

cells: Accepted, image pull or scheduling in progress
At least one container is executing
All containers exited with status zero
All containers stopped, at least one with a non-zero status, and won't be restarted
Pod state could not be obtained from the node

slides.notes: "Walk through a pod pulling a 180 MB image, sitting in Pending for a few seconds, then moving to Running once the container starts. Point out Unknown as a node-communication failure, not a container crash. Exam hook: can a pod go from Failed back to Running."

slides.title: Phases And Transitions
slides.lead: Pod myapp-7f9c6d8b45-k2p9q pulls a 180 MB image in about 6 seconds, then moves to Running once its container starts
slides.notes: "Walk through a pod pulling a 180 MB image, sitting in Pending for a few seconds, then moving to Running once the container starts. Point out Unknown as a node-communication failure, not a container crash. Exam hook: can a pod go from Failed back to Running."

slides.title: Always OnFailure Never
slides.lead: When a container inside a pod exits, the restart policy decides what the kubelet does next, and the right choice depends on whether the workload is long-running or one-off

cells: Restarts on any exit, including success (default)

slides.notes: "Point out Always is the default used by Deployments, which is why web pods come back after a crash. Contrast with Never for a one-time debugging pod that should stay failed for inspection. Exam hook: why Jobs use OnFailure instead of Always."

Mid-session quiz (sections 1-3). Q1. Name two things that break when hundreds of containers are managed by hand. Answer: Any two of placement, health, scaling, updates and discovery. Q2. Which control-plane component is the only direct entry point into the cluster? Answer: The API server. Q3. Which component stores the entire cluster state? Answer: etcd. Q4. What does every container in one pod share? Answer: One IP address, and they can share mounted volumes. Q5. Which container runs once and finishes before the app container starts? Answer: The init container. Q6. Which restart policy is the default? Answer: Always.
Deployments & ReplicaSets: Declarative desired state; replica management; self-healing

slides.title: What A Deployment Is
slides.lead: Manually restarting crashed containers at scale fails, so a Deployment declares the desired state instead of a sequence of steps, and Kubernetes continuously enforces it

points.text: Desired state: declared replica count and container image version
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml submits that declared state

slides.notes: "Explain the shift from issuing commands to declaring an outcome, using the thermostat picture. Interview angle: why does Kubernetes favour declarative over imperative management?"

slides.title: What A Deployment Is

points.text: Declarative state persists continuously, unlike a one-time command
Deployment automatically creates and owns its ReplicaSet

slides.notes: "Explain the shift from issuing commands to declaring an outcome, using the thermostat picture. Interview angle: why does Kubernetes favour declarative over imperative management?"

slides.label: Analogy: water tank with an automatic motor switch
slides.title: What A Deployment Is
slides.notes: TR analogy: A water tank with an automatic motor switch keeps checking the water level. When the level drops, the motor turns on and refills it to full. In the same way, a Deployment keeps checking the pod count and restores it whenever it drops. "Explain the shift from issuing commands to declaring an outcome, using the thermostat picture. Interview angle: why does Kubernetes favour declarative over imperative management?"

slides.title: Reconciliation Loop
slides.lead: A declared target needs an enforcer: the ReplicaSet controller is the continuously running loop that keeps the live pod count equal to what the Deployment declared

points.text: Label selector decides which running pods belong to this set
Reconciliation loop repeatedly compares actual pod count against desired count
Fewer pods than desired: controller creates new ones from the pod template

slides.notes: "Stress that the comparison runs continuously in the background, not once at creation. Mention the label selector is how the controller recognises its own pods. Exam hook: ask what happens if a pod's labels are edited manually."

slides.title: Reconciliation Loop

points.text: More pods than desired: controller terminates the extra matching pods
Deployment manages the ReplicaSet, never pods directly, to allow safe rollouts

slides.notes: "Stress that the comparison runs continuously in the background, not once at creation. Mention the label selector is how the controller recognises its own pods. Exam hook: ask what happens if a pod's labels are edited manually."

slides.title: Pod Loss Recovery
slides.lead: Self-healing is this same reconciliation loop acting without any manual trigger: the moment a running pod disappears, the controller notices the gap

points.text: Deployment web-deployment keeps desired replicas at three
Pod web-deployment-7d9f8c7b67-x4k2p is deleted at 42 seconds uptime
For example by kubectl delete pod
ReplicaSet controller sees actual count two against desired three

slides.notes: "Walk through the crash and replacement using the pod names on the slide. Point at the mismatch between desired and actual count as the trigger. Contrast this with a crashed container, which the kubelet restarts inside the same pod under its restart policy. Exam hook: self-healing replaces pods, it does not resurrect the original one."

slides.title: Pod Loss Recovery

points.text: Scheduler places a new pod on an available healthy node within 5 seconds
Kubelet on that node pulls the image and starts the container

note.text: Within seconds the count returns to three, with a new pod such as web-deployment-7d9f8c7b67-q8z1n replacing the deleted one with no recovery step needed from an administrator

slides.notes: "Walk through the crash and replacement using the pod names on the slide. Point at the mismatch between desired and actual count as the trigger. Contrast this with a crashed container, which the kubelet restarts inside the same pod under its restart policy. Exam hook: self-healing replaces pods, it does not resurrect the original one."

slides.title: Replica Management Live
slides.lead: Keeping replicas alive only matters if their count can change: scaling a Deployment up or down drives the same reconciliation loop toward a new target

points.text: kubectl scale deployment web-deployment --replicas=5 updates the desired count instantly
Amazon EKS console's Workloads tab shows desired versus current replica counts

slides.notes: "Point to the EKS Workloads tab if a screenshot is shown, highlighting desired versus current counts. Mention that rolling updates swap ReplicaSets rather than editing pods in place. Exam hook: ask how a Deployment's rollout differs from a ReplicaSet's scaling."

slides.title: Replica Management Live

points.text: Rolling update replaces pods gradually when a new image is applied
Old ReplicaSet scales down as the new ReplicaSet scales up

note.text: Pods kept alive this way still need one stable address other components can reach, which is the role a stable network identity plays

slides.notes: "Point to the EKS Workloads tab if a screenshot is shown, highlighting desired versus current counts. Mention that rolling updates swap ReplicaSets rather than editing pods in place. Exam hook: ask how a Deployment's rollout differs from a ReplicaSet's scaling."
Services: ClusterIP, NodePort & LoadBalancer; service discovery & stable networking

slides.title: Service Types Map
slides.lead: Pods restart and reschedule constantly, and each new pod gets a fresh IP address, so nothing durable can point at one directly. A Service gives a changing set of pods one stable network identity

points.text: ClusterIP: internal-only access for other pods
NodePort: opens one port on every node
LoadBalancer: provisions an external cloud load balancer
Selector: labels linking a service to its pods

slides.notes: "Open with pod IP churn as the problem a Service solves. Name all three types together before going deep on any one. Interview hook: why Services exist even though pods already have IPs."

slides.title: Default Internal Type
slides.lead: ClusterIP is the default Service type: Kubernetes assigns one stable virtual IP, drawn from the cluster's internal service address range, reachable only from inside the cluster

points.text: Default type when a manifest names none
Virtual IP stays fixed as backend pods change
Used for internal tiers: databases, caches, internal APIs
Never routable from outside the cluster network

slides.notes: "Stress that ClusterIP is the quiet default most workloads use. Give the database-tier example as the everyday case. Exam hook: what type is created when none is specified."

slides.label: Analogy: office internal landline extension
slides.title: Default Internal Type
slides.notes: TR analogy: An office's internal landline extension stays the same even as different employees rotate through that desk: just as a ClusterIP keeps one address while the pods answering it change. "Stress that ClusterIP is the quiet default most workloads use. Give the database-tier example as the everyday case. Exam hook: what type is created when none is specified."

slides.title: Static Node Port
slides.lead: NodePort builds on ClusterIP by also opening one static port, from the default 30000–32767 range, on every node in the cluster

points.text: Reachable via any node's IP plus that port
ClusterIP is still created and used internally
No built-in load balancing across the nodes themselves
External traffic must track which nodes are alive

slides.notes: "Explain NodePort as ClusterIP plus one extra static door on each machine. Mention it is rarely used directly in production clusters. Exam hook: the default NodePort range number."

slides.title: Cloud LB Integration
slides.lead: LoadBalancer extends NodePort further: a cloud-provider controller provisions an external load balancer that forwards traffic onto the NodePort opened on each node

points.text: In Amazon EKS, triggers an AWS load balancer automatically
Standard choice for internet-facing production traffic
Falls back to plain NodePort behaviour outside managed clouds
Health checks stop traffic going to unhealthy nodes

slides.notes: "Point to where this concept lives in practice: the EKS console's load balancer resource created from a Service manifest. Note the per-service cost as a one-line aside. Exam hook: trace what happens behind a LoadBalancer type."

slides.title: DNS And Endpoints
slides.lead: Applications must find a Service without hardcoding its virtual IP, so Kubernetes resolves a stable internal DNS name through CoreDNS, the cluster's built-in DNS server

points.text: Service DNS name follows the pattern service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local for lookup
EndpointSlice objects list the pod IPs matching the selector

slides.notes: "Build on kube-proxy as already known and explain the rules it programs to route a Service IP to a live pod. Say CoreDNS plainly as the modern DNS add-on, not the older kube-dns. Exam hook: how a pod name resolves to a working connection end to end."

slides.title: DNS And Endpoints

points.text: kube-proxy writes iptables or IPVS rules per node
Environment variables also inject service details at pod start

slides.notes: "Build on kube-proxy as already known and explain the rules it programs to route a Service IP to a live pod. Say CoreDNS plainly as the modern DNS add-on, not the older kube-dns. Exam hook: how a pod name resolves to a working connection end to end."

Quiz on Kubernetes Fundamentals. Q1. What does the scheduler decide for each new pod? Answer: Which node it runs on. Q2. What happens to the pods of a node that fails? Answer: The node controller evicts them and Deployment-managed pods are recreated on other nodes. Q3. What is the smallest deployable unit Kubernetes schedules? Answer: The pod. Q4. A ReplicaSet wants three pods and sees two. What does it do? Answer: It creates a new pod from the pod template. Q5. Which Service type is created when a manifest names none? Answer: ClusterIP. Q6. What is the default NodePort range? Answer: 30000 to 32767. Q7. Which cluster add-on resolves a Service name to its ClusterIP? Answer: CoreDNS.
